questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.nclexClientNeeds: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
questions.question: A client has fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and new confusion. What should the RN suspect?
choices: A pattern requiring urgent evaluation for meningitis or other CNS infection
A diagnosis that can be excluded because there is no rash
An expected response to sleeping poorly
A reason to postpone vital-sign assessment
questions.explanation: Fever, headache, neck symptoms, and altered mentation are concerning for CNS infection, although not every patient has every classic feature. Immediate assessment and escalation are needed.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.nclexClientNeeds: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
questions.question: A client with suspected bacterial meningitis is hypotensive and cannot safely undergo lumbar puncture now. What is the best priority?
choices: Delay all treatment until CSF is collected
Give an oral analgesic and discharge
Support stabilization and give prescribed IV antibiotics promptly after feasible blood specimens; do not wait for unsafe LP
Perform LP despite shock to protect culture yield
questions.explanation: Shock is a reason to stabilize before LP, but suspected bacterial meningitis needs urgent antibiotics. Blood cultures are useful when feasible without causing a material treatment delay.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.nclexClientNeeds: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
questions.question: Which statement about head imaging before lumbar puncture is most accurate?
choices: Every person with suspected meningitis must have CT before LP
Imaging is not routine for everyone, but new focal findings, abnormal pupils, or marked neurologic decline may require imaging and specialist review before LP
A normal blood pressure rules out raised ICP
Imaging replaces all blood and CSF tests
questions.explanation: Routine pre-LP neuroimaging can delay care. Specific neurologic red flags or space-occupying lesion concerns alter LP safety and require team-directed imaging and stabilization.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.nclexClientNeeds: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
questions.question: For strongly suspected bacterial meningitis, ordered dexamethasone is ready only after antibiotics are prepared. Which timing principle applies?
choices: Delay antibiotics for several hours until steroid preparation is complete
Never give dexamethasone in any bacterial meningitis
Use dexamethasone instead of antibiotics
Give dexamethasone with or before antibiotics when possible, but never delay antibiotics to wait for it
questions.explanation: Guidance favors early dexamethasone in selected suspected bacterial meningitis, ideally with the first antibiotic dose, while emphasizing that antibiotics must not be delayed.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.nclexClientNeeds: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
questions.question: Which precautions are indicated while meningococcal disease is suspected?
choices: Standard plus Droplet Precautions according to policy
No additional precautions because antibiotics are planned
Airborne isolation for every form of meningitis
Protective neutropenic isolation only
questions.explanation: Suspected meningococcal disease requires Standard plus Droplet Precautions, generally until 24 hours after effective therapy begins. Precautions for other meningitis pathogens vary.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.nclexClientNeeds: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
questions.question: Which healthcare worker exposure most clearly needs infection-prevention review for meningococcal postexposure prophylaxis?
choices: Walking past a closed patient room
Delivering a meal tray without contact with secretions
Unprotected mucous-membrane contact with the patient's respiratory secretions during airway care
Reading the patient's chart at a desk
questions.explanation: Direct unprotected exposure to respiratory secretions is a higher-risk meningococcal contact. Brief non-face-to-face activities do not usually qualify; infection prevention assesses exact circumstances.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.nclexClientNeeds: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
questions.question: A patient with fever, new seizures, confusion, and suspected HSV encephalitis is awaiting MRI and CSF PCR. What treatment should the RN anticipate?
choices: No treatment until every result returns
Prompt prescribed IV acyclovir while evaluation continues
Routine oral acyclovir for every headache
Only droplet precautions without neurologic assessment
questions.explanation: Suspected HSV encephalitis is time-sensitive; ordered IV acyclovir should not wait for complete confirmation when concern is high. Kidney function and treatment response need monitoring.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.nclexClientNeeds: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
questions.question: A patient treated for meningitis develops repeated vomiting, a new unequal pupil, and falling consciousness. What is the priority concern?
choices: Expected harmless sleepiness
Medication adherence only
Normal post-LP discomfort that needs no assessment
Raised intracranial pressure or another acute neurologic complication requiring immediate escalation
questions.explanation: New pupil asymmetry and declining consciousness are neurologic red flags. The RN must reassess airway and perfusion and alert the team for urgent evaluation.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.nclexClientNeeds: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
questions.question: After convulsive activity stops in a patient with encephalitis, awareness remains unexpectedly impaired. Which next step is safest?
choices: Continue serial neurologic assessment and report possible nonconvulsive seizures; EEG may be needed
Assume all confusion is a normal postictal state
Offer oral food to wake the patient
Stop oxygenation and airway monitoring
questions.explanation: Persistent or fluctuating impaired consciousness can reflect nonconvulsive seizures, hypoxia, infection progression, or other causes. Continued assessment and team-directed EEG may be necessary.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.nclexClientNeeds: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
questions.question: Which follow-up assessment is important for a client recovering from bacterial meningitis?
choices: Only whether the fever resolved yesterday
Whether the client remembers the antibiotic name alone
Hearing, cognition, mobility, function, and support needs in addition to infection recovery
No follow-up once antibiotics end
questions.explanation: Bacterial meningitis can leave hearing, cognitive, and functional complications. Recovery planning should assess these domains and arrange individualized rehabilitation or support.
